amendments.rule: The **substantival article** — `הַ` on a participle or adjective used as a noun — takes the pronoun the ASV supplies to make it substantival, and heads on that pronoun rather than on the relative that follows it. `הָרַע` → *that which was evil* is the article with *that which*, headed on *that*; `הָעֹשֶׂה` → *him that doeth* is the article with *him that*, headed on *him*. The supplied pronoun is the article's own rendering and is never `added`. The predicate word keeps its own English, including any copula the ASV supplies, which stays with it under rule 20: in *that which is right*, *is* and *right* belong to the adjective and only *that which* belongs to the article. **An attributive article the ASV renders by a relative goes the same way.** Where `הַ` stands on a participle or adjective modifying an explicit noun and the ASV writes a relative instead of a *the* — `אֹיְבֶיךָ הַקָּמִים עָלֶיךָ` → *thine enemies that rise up against thee*, `הָאִישׁ הָרַךְ` → *The man that is tender*, `הַכְּתוּבִים` → *that are written* — the article takes that relative and heads on it, while the participle or adjective keeps its own English together with any supplied copula, exactly as above. **A demonstrative or possessive determiner the ASV writes in the article's place goes the same way, whatever the article stands on.** Where the ASV writes no *the* for the phrase but a *this*, *that*, *these*, *those*, or a possessive *his*, *her*, *thy*, *thine*, standing where the phrase's *the* would stand — `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness*, `הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thine elder* — that word is what the ASV has written for the article: the article takes it and heads on it, and it is neither `added` nor a reason to mark the article `unrepresented`. **But only where no other morpheme licenses that determiner.** A pronominal suffix standing in the same phrase is rendered by a possessive of its own under rule 18, and where the ASV writes one determiner for the whole phrase the suffix takes it and the article is `unrepresented`: `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* gives *thine* to the suffix on `אָחוֹת` and leaves the article nothing, while `אֲחוֹתַיִךְ הַגְּדֹלוֹת` → *thy sisters, thine elder sisters* writes a determiner for each and the article takes the second. Count the determiners and read which word each stands before, as rule 29 counts the ASV's *the*s. Read what the ASV writes for the article and let that decide which rule governs: a bare *the* is rule 15's ordinary attributive article, a relative or a supplied pronoun is this rule's, a demonstrative or possessive determiner is this rule's too, and where the ASV writes none of them the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29. Where coordinated attributives share a single written relative, the first article takes it and the rest are `unrepresented` under rules 22 and 47.
amendments.why: Rule 41's closing sentence offered a three-way — bare *the*, relative or supplied pronoun, or nothing — and had no place for an article the ASV renders by a determiner. EZK.16 met that case four times and had to reason by analogy: 16.43 `הַזִּמָּה` → *this lewdness* aligned the article to *this* with a note appealing to "rule 41's principle of reading what is written", and 16.61 aligned two articles to *thine* and *thy*, each hedged against the alternative that the determiner is `added`. The corpus carries the reading without contradicting it: 28 units align `הַ` to *this*, 2 to *those*, 4 to *his* and 1 to *her*, and none of them is an `added` determiner beside an `unrepresented` article. The second half is what 16.46 taught against 16.61 — `אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה` → *thine elder sister* has a suffix present that rule 18 already renders by a possessive, so the one written *thine* is the suffix's and the article keeps nothing, exactly as rule 29 and rule 46's first rider let a present morpheme take its English before a supplied one does. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule because the over-broad sentence is the closing three-way itself; a new rule pointing back at it would leave a verse pass reading "where the ASV writes neither the article is `unrepresented`" and marking 16.43's article `unrepresented` with *this* as `added`.

conventions: The אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה formula (16.3, 8, 14, 19, 23, 30, 36, 43, 48, 59, 63) is aligned in three units throughout: אֲדֹנָ takes the ASV's supplied *the* with *Lord*, its 1cs suffix is `unrepresented` because the ASV writes no *my*, and יְהוִה takes *Jehovah*. BSB represents that suffix in all eleven places, which is the whole of the chapter's Sp1cs disagreement count.

Where the ASV renders a comparative by an English comparative adjective, both the מִן and its suffix go `unrepresented`: אֲחוֹתֵךְ הַגְּדוֹלָה מִמֵּךְ -> *thine elder sister* (16.46) and הַגְּדֹלוֹת מִמֵּךְ -> *thine elder sisters* (16.61) write no *than thee* at all. This is rule 30's גָּדַל ... מִן -> *exceeded* case extended to the suffix, and it is distinct from 16.47, 16.51 and 16.52, where the ASV writes *more ... than* and the preposition takes it under rule 25.

An anarthrous noun takes a supplied possessive determiner into its own unit on the same terms as it takes a supplied *the* under rule 29: שָׁדַיִם -> *thy breasts* (16.7) and בְּרֹאשׁ -> *upon thy head* (16.43). No article morpheme is present in either phrase, so nothing else can carry the determiner and it is not `added`.

Rule 31's subtraction was read as putting the head on the noun for שֵׁשׁ -> *fine linen* (16.10, 16.13) and סֹלֶת -> *fine flour* (16.13, 16.19), on the ground that *linen* and *flour* already name the substance and *fine* is the grade specifier added to it -- the תַּנִּין -> *sea monsters* half, not the יַבָּשָׁה -> *dry land* half. The same reading heads עָגִיל -> *ear rings* on *rings* (16.12). These stand beside the chapter's opposite group, where the ASV supplies the generic noun and the head stays on the modifier (רָמָה -> *lofty place*, גַּב -> *vaulted place*, קַדְמָה -> *former estate*, שְׂמֹאל/יָמִין -> *left/right hand*); the two groups are the two halves of one rule and the line between them is which word the ASV supplied.

In בְּנֵי + gentilic proper name rendered by an English plural gentilic -- בְּנֵי מִצְרַיִם -> *the Egyptians* (16.26), בְּנֵי אַשּׁוּר -> *the Assyrians* (16.28) -- the construct בֵּן takes the ASV's single written *the* as a supplied one under rule 29 and the name takes the gentilic, בֵּן's own lexeme being absorbed into it. The construct is not left `unrepresented` and the two morphemes are not fused, since the ASV spends a separate word on each.

report: Checked every candidate bucket with more than one treatment plus the recurring constructions the table is blind to. No verse needs correcting; patches is empty.

The lemma buckets that look split are all ASV-driven: הוּא (thy/thee/thou) follows the case the ASV writes; וְ follows the connective the ASV writes; בְּ and לְ follow the preposition the ASV writes; אֵת is unrepresented in 44 of 49 places and aligned only where the ASV spends a word on the object relation itself (16.8, 16.54, 16.57, 16.59, 16.60), which is rule 16's test applied uniformly.

Constructions verified consistent across every occurrence: אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה (11x), the comparative מִן absorbed into an English comparative adjective (16.46, 16.61) against the comparative the ASV writes out (16.47, 16.51, 16.52), בְּ/לְ + infinitive construct with the complementizer on the preposition and the subject pronoun on the suffix (16.22, 16.30, 16.31, 16.34, 16.52, 16.54, 16.61, 16.63), כַּאֲשֶׁר and לָכֵן fusions with the head on the first morpheme (16.35, 16.37, 16.48, 16.50, 16.59), לִפְנֵי/מִפְּנֵי (16.18, 16.19, 16.50, 16.63), and וְ + לֹא fused as neither/nor with the head on the negative in all six places, including the two lines where the negative is gapped (16.47, 16.48).

Rule 31's two halves are applied consistently and in opposite directions on purpose: where the ASV supplies the generic noun the head sits on the modifier (רָמָה -> lofty place, גַּב -> vaulted place, קַדְמָה -> former estate, שְׂמֹאל -> left hand, אֵלֶּה -> these things, מְעַט -> small matter/little thing), and where it supplies the specifier the head sits on the noun (שֵׁשׁ -> fine linen, סֹלֶת -> fine flour, עָגִיל -> ear rings). The 16.12 head move already in the tree agrees with the second group; nothing else moves.

One near-miss worth naming for the next reader: 16.25 and 16.31 both render a רֹאשׁ ... דֶּרֶךְ chain as *the head of every way* but put the *of* on different tokens. That is licensed by the source, not a split -- 16.25 is אֶל כָּל רֹאשׁ דֶּרֶךְ, where כֹּל is the outer construct and can take no *of*, so the written *of* falls to the rectum דֶּרֶךְ; 16.31 is בְּרֹאשׁ כָּל דֶּרֶךְ, where כֹּל heads the rectum and takes it under rule 19.

BSB: none of the 55 disagreements is a genuine error. The three counted classes are the documented convention differences -- R (18) is prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves bare under rule 40 plus לֵאמֹר's לְ, To (9) is rule 16, Sp1cs (11) is exactly the eleven Adonai suffixes. Of the singletons, 16.11 ה (Sh) is a paragogic he under rule 32 and 16.13's second מְאֹד is a repetition under rule 22, both of which BSB attaches to the host word by convention. The one worth a second look, 16.63 יִהְיֶה, is right: the ASV recasts וְלֹא יִהְיֶה לָךְ עוֹד פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה as *never open thy mouth any more*, and every English word is already owned -- never by לֹא, open by פִּתְחוֹן, mouth by פֶּה, thy by the suffix, any more by עוֹד -- so nothing is left for the existential.

The validation report's 33 repeated notes are mostly bare rule citations ("Rule 16.", "Rule 18.", "Rule 31.") and need no log entry. The five that carry an actual chapter judgment are recorded in conventions below.

Contract: one amendment, to rule 41. The chapter met three articles the ASV renders by a determiner rather than a *the* or a relative (16.43 this, 16.61 thine and thy) and one it leaves unrepresented because a suffix in the same phrase already licenses the determiner (16.46). Rule 41's closing three-way did not cover that case, and 16.43's note had to reason from "rule 41's principle of reading what is written" -- so the sentence is widened where it stands rather than pointed at from a new rule.
